# Purpose and how to use this document

This Part I document estimates a linear trend in the supplied annual temperature record and examines its residuals. It includes gap-aware plots, autocorrelation diagnostics, a Durbin–Watson Monte Carlo test, and a Breusch–Pagan test. Structural-change estimation, bootstrap inference, and the Monte Carlo comparison remain future work in Parts II and III.

This document contains the statistical code, explanations, tables, figures, interpretation and independent checks all in one place.


```{r setup, include=FALSE}
input_path <- knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)
project_root <- normalizePath(dirname(input_path), mustWork = TRUE)
stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(project_root, "Station08.csv")))
artifact_root <- file.path(project_root, "work", "main_rmd_run")
for (folder in c("figures", "tables", "work/simulation", "outputs", "knitr_figures")) {
  dir.create(file.path(artifact_root, folder), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = artifact_root)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE, error = FALSE, cache = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center", fig.path = paste0(file.path(artifact_root, "knitr_figures"), "/")
)
options(knitr.graphics.rel_path = FALSE)
fmt <- function(value, digits = 4) {
  formatC(value, digits = digits, format = "f")
}
write_csv <- function(x, file) {
  write.csv(x, file, row.names = FALSE, na = "")
}
```

# 1 Model Specification and Notes

This report starts with the model
$$y_i=\beta_0 + \beta_1t_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i=1, \ldots,n,$$
where $i$ is observation position and $t_i$ is the transformed calendar years:
$$t_i = (\mathrm{Year}_i - 1900)/10.$$
**On rescaling time:** The year-1900 centering is retained. The intercept is the fitted linear model temperature at 1900, and the slope is expressed in degrees Celsius per decade. Centering changes the intercept's reference year but not the slope or fitted curve. Appendix 1 explains this choice.

**On data completeness** There are 226 observations covering 261 calendar years from 1753-2013, with 35 missing years across five gaps. The largest gap is **1981- 2009**, comprising 29 unobserved years. Observation position and calendar time therefore differ. We retain every supplied observation, preserve calendar spacing,  and explain which diagnostics use each kind of lag.


# 2 Data Loading and Diagnosis of the Gap Structure

```{r load-data}
master_seed <- 20260926L
set.seed(master_seed)

library(ggplot2)

dat <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "Station08.csv"))
stopifnot(identical(names(dat), c("Year", "Temperature")),
          nrow(dat) == 226L, !anyNA(dat),
          all(is.finite(dat$Year)), all(is.finite(dat$Temperature)),
          !anyDuplicated(dat$Year))

# Sort by year, validate supplied data instead of silently dropping observations.
dat <- dat[order(dat$Year), ]
stopifnot(all(diff(dat$Year)>0))
n <- nrow(dat)

cat("Number of observations n =", n, "\n")
cat("First year:", min(dat$Year), " Last year:", max(dat$Year), "\n")
```

```{r gap-detection}
# ---- Gap diagnostics: locate every "year jump" ----
full_years     <- seq(min(dat$Year), max(dat$Year))
missing_years  <- setdiff(full_years, dat$Year)
# year difference between consecutive observations
gap_len        <- diff(dat$Year)
# a difference > 1 indicates a gap
gap_start_idx  <- which(gap_len > 1)

gap_table <- data.frame(
  from      = dat$Year[gap_start_idx],
  to        = dat$Year[gap_start_idx + 1],
  n_missing = gap_len[gap_start_idx] - 1
)

print(gap_table)
cat("\nTotal missing years:", length(missing_years), "\n")
cat("Number of gaps:", nrow(gap_table), "\n")
big_gap <- gap_table[which.max(gap_table$n_missing), ]
cat("Largest gap:", big_gap$n_missing, "years, from", big_gap$from, "to", big_gap$to, "\n")
```

The data confirm **5 gaps totaling 35 missing years**, the vast majority
of which is the 29-year gap from 1981–2009. This means that two
observations that are adjacent in "sequence position" are not
necessarily adjacent in calendar time — this is the fundamental reason
why the ACF and DW test below require special handling.

To ensure that every subsequent time-connected plot is not misleading,
we construct a "contiguous year segment" label here: only observations
adjacent within the same segment will be connected by a line.

```{r segment-and-t}
# Increment the segment id by 1 whenever the year jumps by more than 1 year; used to avoid drawing lines across gaps
dat$segment <- c(1, cumsum(diff(dat$Year) > 1) + 1)

# Centered, decade-scaled time index
dat$t <- (dat$Year - 1900) / 10
```

# 3. Exploratory Analysis

```{r explore-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = Temperature)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(group = segment), linewidth = 0.4, colour = "steelblue4") +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = "steelblue4") +
  labs(
    title = "Station08 annual mean temperature (1753-2013)",
    subtitle = "Grey shading = largest data gap (1981-2009, no observations)",
    x = "Year", y = "Annual mean temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r explore-stats}
cat("Temperature range:", round(range(dat$Temperature), 2), "\n")
cat("5 coldest years:\n")
print(head(dat[order(dat$Temperature), c("Year", "Temperature")], 5))
cat("5 warmest years:\n")
print(tail(dat[order(dat$Temperature), c("Year", "Temperature")], 5))
cat("Standard deviation before 1900:", round(sd(dat$Temperature[dat$Year < 1900]), 3),
    "  Standard deviation from 1900 onward:", round(sd(dat$Temperature[dat$Year >= 1900]), 3), "\n")
```

**Main features:**

- **Direction of the fitted trend:** Temperatures show considerable annual variability and a modest positive full-sample linear slope. This station alone cannot establish a global trend or its cause.
- **Interannual variability:** The sample standard deviation is about 0.70°C. Year-to-year variation is substantial relative to the fitted long-run change.
- **Unusual observations:** The coldest observed year is 1851, at about 7.65°C; the warmest is 2011, at 11.73°C. These observations are retained. Part II includes a descriptive check omitting the coldest year.
- **Missing decades:** The four 2010–2013 observations follow the 29-year absence of data. They do not show whether warming was gradual, accelerated, or interrupted during the gap. We do not infer a temperature discontinuity from the absence of observations.


# 4. OLS Estimation of the Linear Trend

```{r ols-fit}
trend_model <- lm(Temperature ~ t, data = dat)
summary(trend_model)

print(coef(trend_model))
cat("R-squared:", round(summary(trend_model)$r.squared, 4), "\n")

beta0_hat <- coef(trend_model)[1]
beta1_hat <- coef(trend_model)[2]

cat("Estimated intercept (fitted temperature around year 1900):", round(beta0_hat, 3), "°C\n")
cat("Estimated slope:", round(beta1_hat, 4), "°C per decade\n")
cat("Converted to per century:", round(beta1_hat * 10, 3), "°C per century\n")

```

```{r ols-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
dat$fitted_linear <- fitted(trend_model)

ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = Temperature)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(group = segment), linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_linear), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Geneva temperature series with OLS linear trend",
       x = "Year", y = "Annual mean temperature (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

**Interpretation:** $\hat\beta_0 = 9.617°C$ is the model-implied
"average" temperature level around the year 1900;
$\hat\beta_1 = 0.0337°C$ per decade (about 0.337°C per century)
represents the estimated long-run linear warming rate.
$R^2 \approx 0.105$, indicating that the deterministic trend explains
only about 10.5% of the total variation, with the vast majority of
interannual variability remaining in the residuals — consistent with the
impression from the exploratory analysis that "interannual variability
far exceeds the change due to the trend."

**On the impact of the gaps:** Using actual calendar year preserves the meaning of the slope; OLS can be computed for an unevenly spaced fixed design. Missing years nevertheless affect which periods are represented and can affect estimates, precision and interpretation. Exogeneity of the errors and the missingness mechanism cannot be verified from the CSV. The 222 observations through 1980 also inform the fitted slope; it is not determined solely by a contrast between two endpoint groups. A single linear slope averages across the observed record and does not identify what happened within the missing decades. As required in Part I, we do not draw a slope-significance conclusion here.


# 3. Residual Diagnostics

```{r residuals}
dat$residual    <- residuals(trend_model)
dat$residual_sq <- dat$residual^2
```

## Residuals over Time

```{r resid-time-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = residual)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(group = segment), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Residuals from the linear trend model", x = "Year", y = "Residual (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The residuals fluctuate around zero, with runs of similarly signed values and low-frequency departures from the linear fit. These patterns suggest residual dependence and possible inadequacy of the constant-trend mean. We inspect both observation-lag and calendar-lag ACFs, then use Monte Carlo calibration for the assigned DW statistic.

## Residual Autocorrelation Function (ACF) — Observation and Calendar Lags



**Why the lag definition matters:** Applied to the observed residual vector, `acf()` measures lag by row position. It is a valid description of dependence between observed rows, but a one-observation lag is not always a one-calendar-year lag. For example, observations `r match(1980, dat$Year)` and `r match(2010, dat$Year)` correspond to 1980 and 2010, thirty calendar years apart.

**Calendar-lag comparison:** Place residuals on the full calendar grid, insert `NA` for unobserved years, and use `na.action = na.pass`. This uses available pairs for each calendar lag without imputing temperatures. With missing values, the resulting estimates need not define a valid autocorrelation sequence; the usual plot bounds are descriptive rather than calibrated inference. Both ACFs are retained, and their lag meanings are stated explicitly.


```{r acf-compare, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
# Naive approach (uncorrected, shown only for comparison to illustrate the problem)
acf_naive <- acf(dat$residual, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)

# Corrected approach: place back on the full calendar grid + na.action = na.pass
res_full <- rep(NA_real_, length(full_years))
res_full[match(dat$Year, full_years)] <- dat$residual
res_ts   <- ts(res_full, start = min(full_years), frequency = 1)
acf_gap  <- acf(res_ts, na.action = na.pass, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(acf_naive, main = "ACF by observation lag")
plot(acf_gap,   main = "ACF by calendar-year lag")

cat("Observation-lag 1 autocorrelation:", round(acf_naive$acf[2], 3), "\n")
cat("Calendar-lag 1 autocorrelation:", round(acf_gap$acf[2], 3), "\n")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

The first observation-lag and calendar-lag autocorrelations are `r fmt(as.numeric(acf_naive$acf[2]), 3)` and `r fmt(as.numeric(acf_gap$acf[2]), 3)`. They are close here because most observed pairs are consecutive calendar years. Both indicate positive short-range residual dependence. Their similarity in this dataset does not make the two lag definitions interchangeable in general.


## Residual Variance over Time

```{r variance-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = Year, y = residual_sq)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = big_gap$from, xmax = big_gap$to,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(
    title = "Squared residuals over time",
    subtitle = "Caution: the smooth line is not supported by any observations inside the shaded region",
    x = "Year", y = expression(hat(epsilon)[t]^2)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The scatter uses actual calendar years. The loess curve is a descriptive smooth, and its portion inside the long gap is not supported by observations from those years. The final four observations can influence its endpoint behavior; the plot cannot establish how variance evolved during the gap. No formal conclusion about constant variance follows from this smooth alone.


## Normal QQ Plot of Residuals

```{r qq-plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
qqnorm(dat$residual, main = "Normal QQ plot of residuals")
qqline(dat$residual)
```

The QQ plot is broadly linear in its center, with some tail departures. This is compatible with a Gaussian approximation but does not verify normality. Time spacing does not enter the QQ construction, although the plotted marginal distribution still reflects only the observed years. Gaussian errors remain an explicit reference assumption for the DW Monte Carlo calibration.

# 4. Testing for First-Order Residual Autocorrelation: Durbin–Watson Monte Carlo Test
**Primary assigned statistic:** The handout defines

$$d_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{\sum_{i=2}^n(\widehat e_i-\widehat e_{i-1})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n\widehat e_i^2}.$$

Its adjacency is by observation position. We implement this definition as the primary test and interpret it accordingly. Calendar gaps affect its meaning, but restricting its numerator to calendar-adjacent pairs would define a different statistic rather than implement the assigned one.

**Retained calendar-gap sensitivity:**  original variant is kept:

$$d_{\mathrm{calendar}}=\frac{\sum_{i:\ s_{i+1}-s_i=1}(\widehat e_{i+1}-\widehat e_i)^2}{\sum_i\widehat e_i^2}.$$

It includes only genuinely adjacent calendar years. Both statistics can be written as $e'Ae/e'e$, with different difference matrices. Each is calibrated using its own formula and the same observed regression design.


```{r dw-define}
# Naive DW (uncorrected, shown only for comparison)
dw_naive_stat <- function(e) sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2)
d_obs_naive <- dw_naive_stat(dat$residual)

# ---- Gap-sensitive DW: only compute differences over pairs that are truly calendar-adjacent (year difference = 1) ----
valid_pairs <- which(diff(dat$Year) == 1)      # indices of valid "adjacent pairs"
m_pairs <- length(valid_pairs)

Dmat <- matrix(0, nrow = m_pairs, ncol = n)
for (k in seq_len(m_pairs)) {
  i <- valid_pairs[k]
  Dmat[k, i]     <- -1
  Dmat[k, i + 1] <-  1
}
A_gap <- crossprod(Dmat)   # A = D'D

dw_gap_stat <- function(e) as.numeric((t(e) %*% A_gap %*% e) / (t(e) %*% e))
d_obs_gap <- dw_gap_stat(dat$residual)
d_obs <- d_obs_naive  # primary statistic: assignment definition

cat("Assigned observation-adjacency DW:", round(d_obs_naive, 4), "\n")
cat("Gap-sensitive DW statistic:", round(d_obs_gap, 4), "\n")
cat("Valid calendar-adjacent year pairs used:", m_pairs, "/", n - 1, "sequence-adjacent pairs\n")

```

The assigned statistic is `r fmt(d_obs)`, and the calendar-adjacent variant is `r fmt(d_obs_gap)`. There are `r m_pairs` calendar-adjacent pairs among the `r n-1` observation-adjacent pairs. Both are reported, with the assigned statistic governing the main Part I conclusion.

## Design of the Monte Carlo Test

Under the specified null $\varepsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2I_n)$, the fitted residuals are $e=M_X\varepsilon$, where $M_X=I-X(X'X)^{-1}X'$. Regression coefficients disappear after projection and error scale cancels in $e'Ae/e'e$. Thus the null law is determined by the fixed design and the chosen difference matrix.

We retain projection and simulation loop. Each standard-normal draw is evaluated using **both** DW definitions. Separate lower and upper empirical critical values give the two tails; they are not obtained by reflecting one tail around two. The previous Rmd’s interpolated type-7 critical-value quantiles are retained. Simulation approximates the specified finite-sample Gaussian law, rather than an unrestricted null of every process without first-order correlation.


```{r dw-mc-test}
X <- model.matrix(trend_model)
H <- X %*% solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X)
M <- diag(n) - H

set.seed(master_seed)
B <- 9999L
d_sim <- d_sim_gap <- numeric(B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  eps_star <- rnorm(n)
  e_star <- as.numeric(M %*% eps_star)
  d_sim[b] <- dw_naive_stat(e_star)   # assigned observation-adjacency statistic
  d_sim_gap[b] <- dw_gap_stat(e_star) # retained calendar-adjacent sensitivity
}

alpha <- 0.05
crit_lower <- unname(quantile(d_sim, alpha / 2, type = 7))
crit_upper <- unname(quantile(d_sim, 1 - alpha / 2, type = 7))
p_lower_adj <- (sum(d_sim <= d_obs) + 1) / (B + 1)
p_upper_adj <- (sum(d_sim >= d_obs) + 1) / (B + 1)
p_val_dw <- min(1, 2 * min(p_lower_adj, p_upper_adj))

crit_gap <- unname(quantile(d_sim_gap, c(alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2), type = 7))
p_val_dw_gap <- min(1, 2 * min(
  (sum(d_sim_gap <= d_obs_gap) + 1) / (B + 1),
  (sum(d_sim_gap >= d_obs_gap) + 1) / (B + 1)
))
dw_results <- data.frame(
  Definition = c("Assigned: observation adjacency", "Sensitivity: calendar adjacency"),
  Statistic = c(d_obs, d_obs_gap),
  Lower_2_5_percent = c(crit_lower, crit_gap[1]),
  Upper_97_5_percent = c(crit_upper, crit_gap[2]),
  Equal_tail_p_value = c(p_val_dw, p_val_dw_gap)
)
knitr::kable(dw_results, digits = 4)

# Optional packaged cross-check uses its own statistic/reference and is not the primary calibration.
if (requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(lmtest::dwtest(trend_model))
}

```

**Results and conclusion:** The assigned statistic is `r fmt(d_obs)`, with lower and upper cutoffs `r fmt(crit_lower)` and `r fmt(crit_upper)` and equal-tail p-value `r fmt(p_val_dw)`. It falls below the lower cutoff. The calendar-adjacent sensitivity also rejects in the positive-dependence direction, with p-value `r fmt(p_val_dw_gap)`. These results agree with the residual and ACF plots. Rejection challenges the specified independent Gaussian linear-model errors; departures in the mean specification can also contribute to residual patterns.


# 5. Testing for Heteroskedasticity: Breusch–Pagan Test

The auxiliary regression

$$\widehat e_i^2=\gamma_0+\gamma_1t_i+v_i$$

tests for a **linear variance trend**, using the requested statistic $BP=nR^2$ and nominal $\chi^2_1$ reference. A zero time coefficient is a narrow diagnostic null; non-rejection does not establish homoskedasticity against every possible variance pattern.

**On gaps and calibration:** The regression uses actual transformed calendar year and does not require equally spaced rows for its algebra. Missing periods still limit interpretation, and the detected residual dependence weakens the usual asymptotic chi-square reference. This limitation is separate from the choice of observation versus calendar adjacency in DW and ACF.


```{r bp-test}
aux_model <- lm(residual_sq ~ t, data = dat)
R2_aux   <- summary(aux_model)$r.squared
BP_stat  <- n * R2_aux
p_val_bp <- pchisq(BP_stat, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

cat("Breusch-Pagan statistic BP:", round(BP_stat, 4), "\n")
cat("Degrees of freedom:", 1, "\n")
cat("BP p-value:", round(p_val_bp, 4), "\n")

# Previous cross-check: bptest(trend_model, varformula = ~ t, data = dat)
# Optional cross-check; no dependency on lmtest for the main result.
if (requireNamespace("lmtest", quietly = TRUE)) {
  print(lmtest::bptest(trend_model, varformula = ~ t, data = dat))
}

```

**Result:** $BP=$ `r fmt(BP_stat)` and the nominal p-value is `r fmt(p_val_bp)`. We do not reject a linear variance trend at 5%. This is compatible with the descriptive plot but does not prove constant variance, especially given the residual dependence.


# 6. Comparing the Inferential Principles

The main distinction is the **reference assumptions**, not whether residuals are squared.

- **DW under a specified Gaussian null:** Residual projection removes the regression coefficients, and the ratio of quadratic forms removes scale. Conditional on the observed design and difference matrix, standard-normal simulation therefore generates the specified finite-sample reference law. A finite simulation estimates its quantiles; separate corrected tail counts give the reported Monte Carlo p-value.
- **BP with the requested chi-square reference:** The usual $nR^2$ calibration is asymptotic and needs its regularity conditions. Under a broader homoskedastic null, the error distribution, higher moments and dependence are not fully specified.
- **Gaussian Monte Carlo BP is also possible:** If the same independent Gaussian error law is imposed, project standard-normal draws, square their residuals and recompute the auxiliary $R^2$. Multiplying all residuals by an error scale multiplies all squared residuals by its square and leaves this $R^2$ unchanged. Thus Gaussian simulation can also calibrate BP conditional on the design. The nonlinear squaring step does not prevent this. The issue is that imposing Gaussian independence is stronger than assuming homoskedasticity alone.

Here we retain the assignment's asymptotic chi-square BP calculation and qualify it in light of dependence rather than treating non-rejection as proof of constant variance.


# 7. Overall Assessment of the Initial Model
Bringing the graphical and formal diagnostics together:

1. **Positive descriptive slope:** The full-sample linear estimate is `r fmt(beta1_hat)`°C per decade, with $R^2=$ `r fmt(summary(trend_model)$r.squared, 3)`. This is a modest average fitted change, not a Part I significance claim.
2. **Gaussian reference remains an assumption:** The QQ plot is broadly linear in its center with tail departures; it does not verify normality.
3. **No detected linear variance trend:** The nominal BP p-value is `r fmt(p_val_bp)`. Non-rejection does not establish homoskedasticity, and dependence qualifies the reference law.
4. **Residual dependence matters:** Both DW variants and both ACFs indicate positive residual dependence. Ordinary independent-error OLS standard errors are not a reliable basis for the requested later inference without addressing this issue. A richer mean may reduce, but need not eliminate, the residual pattern.
5. **Missing periods constrain interpretation:** Actual calendar spacing is retained, but there is no direct evidence about temperatures during 1981–2009. The missingness mechanism and station measurement history are unknown.

**Conclusion for Part I:** The linear model is a useful starting description. Its residual patterns motivate a continuous change in slope and a bootstrap that can retain dependence. Parts II–III below carry out that inference and evaluate its finite-sample behavior.

# 8. Structural Change and Boostrap Inderence (Part II)

```{r part2-setup}
x <- dat$t
m0 <- trend_model
e0 <- dat$residual
seed <- master_seed
B_test <- 9999L
B_ci <- 4999L
B_dw <- B
simulation_M <- 1000L
simulation_B <- 499L
dw <- d_obs
dwcrit <- c(crit_lower, crit_upper)
dwp<-p_val_dw
bp<- BP_stat
bpp <- p_val_bp
ncores<- parallel::detectCores()
if (is.na(ncores)) ncores <- 1L
stopifnot(is.logical(params$recompute_simulation),
          length(params$recompute_simulation) == 1L,
```


## Continuous broken trend and admissible dates

 For each candidate observation $k$, we are estimating
 
 $$y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \delta(x_i - x_k)_+ + \varepsilon_i, \qquad (z)_+=\max(0,z). $$
 The hinge is zero at the break, so the fitted temperature remains continous. Before the break the slope is $\beta$, after it the slope is $\beta + \delta$. The model changes slope without an instantenous level jump.

Fifteen-percent trimming gives candidate positions from $\lceil .15n\rceil$ to $\lfloor .85n\rfloor$. Trimming uses observation positions, while the regressors use calendar time. For efficient repeated searches, residualize each candidate hinge against the linear regressors and normalize it. Its squared projection onto the null residuals equals the reduction in RSS from adding that hinge. This is the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell identity, and later checks compare it with explicit OLS searches.


```{r prepare-break-design}
 prepare_design <- function(year,trim=0.15){
   stopifnot(is.numeric(year), all(is.finite(year)), length(year) >= 10L,
             all(diff(year)>0),
             length(trim)==1L, trim>0, trim<0.5)
   n<-length(year)
   x<-(year - mean(year))/10
   X0 <- cbind(intercept = 1, pre = x)
   qr0<- qr(X0)
   Q0 <- qr.Q(qr0)
   index<-seq.int(ceiling(trim*n), floor((1-trim)*n))
   H <- outer(x,x[index], function(a,b) pmax(0,a-b))
   Hres <- H - Q0 %*% crossprod(Q0,H)
   hnorm <- sqrt(colSums(Hres^2))
   stopifnot(all(hnorm>0))
   Qhinge<-sweep(Hres,2L, hnorm, "/")
   structure(list(year = year, n=n, x=x, X0=X0, qr0 = qr0, Q0=Q0, index=index, candidates=index, H=H, Qhinge=Qhinge, hinge_norm = hnorm, trim=trim), class = "break_design")
 }
```
The optimized search accepts one response vector or a matrix with one bootstrap response per column. The assignment statistic is

$$F_T=RSS_0-\min_{k\in\mathcal K}RSS_1(k).$$

Despite its label, this is **raw RSS reduction**, in °C squared, rather than a conventional variance-normalized F ratio. The helper also returns a normalized version for completeness, but that field is not used for the reported tests. Ties use the first candidate.

```{r break-statistic-and-fit}
break_statistics <- function(y, design){
  if(is.null(dim(y))) y<-matrix(y, ncol = 1L)
  stopifnot(nrow(y) == design$n, all(is.finite(y)))
  resid0<-y-design$Q0 %*% crossprod(design$Q0,y)
  rss0 <- colSums(resid0^2)
  scores2 <- crossprod(design$Qhinge, resid0)^2
  best<- max.col(t(scores2), ties.method = "first")
  gain <- scores2[cbind(best, seq_len(ncol(y)))]
  rss1 <- pmax(rss0 - gain, .Machine$double.eps * pmax(rss0,1))
  list(F=gain, studentized_F = gain / (rss1/(design$n - 3L)),
  grid_index= best, RSS0 = rss0, RSS1= rss1, gain = gain)
}

fit_break <- function(y,design){
  stopifnot(is.numeric(y), length(y) == design$n, all(is.finite(y)))
  stats<- break_statistics(y,design)
  j<-stats$grid_index[1L]
  X1 <- cbind(design$X0, delta = design$H[, j])
  fit<- lm.fit(X1,y)
  co <- fit$coefficients
  co <- c(intercept = unname(co[1L]), pre=unname(co[2L]), delta = unname(co[3L]), 
          post = unname(co[2L] + co[3L]))
  null<- lm.fit(design$X0, y)
  list(F = unname(stats$F[1L]), index=design$index[j], year=design$year[design$index[j]], coef = co,
         pre = co[["pre"]], delta = co[["delta"]], post = co[["post"]],
       fitted = fit$fitted.values, residuals = fit$residuals,
       null_fitted = null$fitted.values, null_residuals = null$residuals,
       null_coef = null$coefficients, RSS0 = unname(stats$RSS0[1L]),
       RSS1 = unname(stats$RSS1[1L]))

}
```


```{r search-observed-break}
design <- prepare_design(year)
candidates<-design$index
# This explicit lm loop also provides an independent validation of the fast search.
rss<-sapply(candidates,function(k) sum(resid(lm(y~x+I(pmax(0,x-x[k]))))^2))
k<-candidates[which.min(rss)]; h<-pmax(0,x-x[k]); X1<-cbind(1,x,h)
m1<-lm(y~x+h); e1<-resid(m1); theta<-c(pre=coef(m1)[2],post=sum(coef(m1)[2:3]))
Fobs<-sum(e0^2)-min(rss)
fast<-fit_break(y,design)
stopifnot(abs(fast$F-Fobs)<1e-8)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  First_index = min(candidates), Last_index = max(candidates),
  First_year = year[min(candidates)], Last_year = year[max(candidates)],
  Selected_index = k, Selected_year = year[k],
  Linear_RSS = sum(e0^2), Broken_RSS = min(rss), Raw_RSS_reduction = Fobs
), digits = 4)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Pre-break slope", "Slope change", "Post-break slope"),
  Estimate = c(unname(coef(m1)[2]), unname(coef(m1)[3]), unname(sum(coef(m1)[2:3])))
), digits = 4)
```
The search covers positions `r min(candidates)`–`r max(candidates)`, or years `r year[min(candidates)]`–`r year[max(candidates)]`. It selects `r year[k]`, with $F_T=$ `r fmt(Fobs)`. The pre-break slope is `r fmt(coef(m1)[2])`, the change is `r fmt(coef(m1)[3])`, and the post-break slope is `r fmt(sum(coef(m1)[2:3]))` °C per decade.

The fitted equation retains year-1900 reference:

$$\widehat y_i = `r fmt(coef(m1)[1])` + (`r fmt(coef(m1)[2])`)t_i
+ (`r fmt(coef(m1)[3])`)(t_i-t_{\widehat k})_+,$$

where $t_i=(\mathrm{Year}_i-1900)/10$ and $t_{\widehat k}=(`r year[k]`-1900)/10$.
The broken-model intercept is the extrapolated pre-break line at 1900. It is not the fitted temperature there, because the hinge is already positive at that year.


Selecting the best date improves fit by construction. Under $H_0:\delta=0$, the date is unidentified. A usual fixed-date test does not account for the search. The date here is a descriptive optimum until the entire selection procedure is calibrated under the no-break null.

## Bootstrap error generators

The IID residual bootstrap samples centered residuals with replacement. It targets independent, identically distributed errors. The independent wild bootstrap multiplies each residual by an independent Rademacher sign, retaining its location-specific squared magnitude but removing serial dependence.

The primary dependent wild bootstrap (DWB) uses correlated Gaussian multipliers:

$$w_1\sim N(0,1),\quad a_i=\exp[-(s_i-s_{i-1})/\ell],\quad
w_i=a_iw_{i-1}+\sqrt{1-a_i^2}z_i,$$

where $z_i$ are independent standard Gaussians. This gives
$\operatorname{Cov}(w_i,w_j)=\exp(-|s_i-s_j|/\ell)$.
Using actual calendar gaps weakens multiplier dependence across missing years without imputing temperatures. The multiplier correlation is a chosen dependence approximation, not a fitted error autocorrelation.

Residuals are centered and multiplied by $\sqrt{n/(n-p)}$: $p=2$ for the linear null and $p=3$ for the fitted broken alternative. This offsets residual shrinkage from estimating the linear coefficients. The primary bandwidth is six years, approximately $\operatorname{round}(n^{1/3})$.

```{r dependent-wild-weights}
dwb_weights <- function(design, B, ell = round(design$n^(1/3))) {
  stopifnot(B >= 1L, ell > 0)
  w <- matrix(rnorm(design$n * B), nrow = design$n, ncol = B)
  a <- exp(-diff(design$year) / ell)
  for (i in 2L:design$n)
    w[i, ] <- a[i - 1L] * w[i - 1L, ] + sqrt(1 - a[i - 1L]^2) * w[i, ]
  w
}
```

```{r bootstrap-error-generator}
bootstrap_errors <- function(e, year, B, method, ell = 6, df = 2) {
  n <- length(e)
  stopifnot(length(year) == n, n > df, all(is.finite(e)),
            all(is.finite(year)), B >= 1L,
            length(method) == 1L, method %in% c("iid", "wild", "dwb"))
  e <- (e - mean(e)) * sqrt(n / (n - df))
  switch(method,
    iid = matrix(sample(e, n * B, replace = TRUE), nrow = n),
    wild = e * matrix(2L * sample.int(2L, n * B, replace = TRUE) - 3L,
                      nrow = n),
    dwb = e * dwb_weights(list(n = n, year = year), B, ell))
}
```

## Test the no-break null

For a break test, bootstrap samples must impose the no-break null. Fit the linear model, generate $e_i^*$ from its residuals, and form $y_i^*=\widehat y_{0i}+e_i^*$. Refit the null and search every admissible break in each draw. Because the linear mean lies in the projected-out space, evaluating the statistic on $e^*$ alone is algebraically identical and faster.

The 95% critical value uses the type-1 empirical quantile. The corrected upper-tail probability is

$$p=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^B\mathbf 1\{F_{T,b}^*\ge F_T\}}{B+1}.$$

Reject at 5% when $p\le .05$. The reusable function below implements this algorithm; the empirical chunks also preserve all simulated statistics for plotting. The same function is used in Part III.
```{r bootstrap-test-function}
bootstrap_break <- function(y, design, B = 999L,
                            methods = c("iid", "wild", "dwb"),
                            seed = NULL, ell = round(design$n^(1/3)),
                            level = 0.05, keep_statistics = FALSE) {
  B <- as.integer(B)
  stopifnot(B >= 1L, level > 0, level < 1,
            length(methods) > 0, all(methods %in% c("iid", "wild", "dwb")),
            !anyDuplicated(methods))
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  observed <- fit_break(y, design)
  # Null-restricted residuals enforce the hypothesis in every bootstrap draw.
  # Degrees-of-freedom correction offsets shrinkage from estimating two terms.
  e <- observed$null_residuals
  results <- vector("list", length(methods)); names(results) <- methods
  for (method in methods) {
    boot_errors <- bootstrap_errors(e, design$year, B, method, ell, df = 2)
    # Adding the fitted null trend leaves this residual-projection statistic
    # unchanged, so computing directly from bootstrap errors is exact.
    Fstar <- break_statistics(boot_errors, design)$F
    p <- (1 + sum(Fstar >= observed$F)) / (B + 1)
    result <- list(method = method, F = observed$F, p_value = p,
                   critical = unname(quantile(Fstar, 1 - level, type = 1)),
                   reject = p <= level, B = B, level = level,
                   ell = if (method == "dwb") ell else NA_real_)
    if (keep_statistics) result$statistics <- Fstar
    results[[method]] <- result
  }
  list(observed = observed, results = results)
}
```

```{r empirical-bootstrap-tests}
methods <- c("iid", "wild", "dwb")

btests <- list()

draws <- list()

for (j in seq_along(methods)) {
    set.seed(seed + 100L + j)
    err <- bootstrap_errors(e0, year, B_test, method = methods[j], ell = 6, df = 2)
    fs <- break_statistics(err, design)$F
    draws[[methods[j]]] <- fs
    btests[[j]] <- data.frame(method = methods[j], ell = ifelse(methods[j] == "dwb", 6, NA), 
        B = B_test, statistic = Fobs, critical95 = quantile(fs, 0.95, type = 1, names = FALSE), 
        p_value = (1 + sum(fs >= Fobs))/(B_test + 1), exceedances = sum(fs >= Fobs))
}

for (ell in c(3L, 12L)) {
    set.seed(seed + 200L + ell)
    err <- bootstrap_errors(e0, year, B_test, method = "dwb", ell = ell, df = 2)
    fs <- break_statistics(err, design)$F
    btests[[length(btests) + 1]] <- data.frame(method = "dwb", ell = ell, B = B_test, statistic = Fobs, 
        critical95 = quantile(fs, 0.95, type = 1, names = FALSE), p_value = (1 + sum(fs >= 
            Fobs))/(B_test + 1), exceedances = sum(fs >= Fobs))
}

btests <- do.call(rbind, btests)

write_csv(btests, "tables/bootstrap_tests.csv")

```

```{r bootstrap-test-table}
bootstrap_table <- btests
bootstrap_table$Procedure <- c("IID residual", "Independent wild", "Dependent wild: ell=6",
                               "Dependent wild: ell=3", "Dependent wild: ell=12")
bootstrap_table$Decision <- ifelse(bootstrap_table$p_value <= .05, "Reject", "Do not reject")
knitr::kable(bootstrap_table[, c("Procedure", "B", "statistic", "critical95", "p_value", "Decision")],
             digits = 4, caption = "Unknown-break tests and dependent-wild bandwidth sensitivity")
```

Each row uses `r B_test` bootstrap draws. Primary DWB ($\ell=6$) gives $p=$ `r fmt(btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & btests$ell == 6 & !is.na(btests$ell)])`, rejecting at 5%. The longer bandwidth ($\ell=12$) gives `r fmt(btests$p_value[btests$method == "dwb" & btests$ell == 12 & !is.na(btests$ell)])`, which does not reject. Thus the evidence is bandwidth sensitive.

Both independent-error methods have zero exceedances and p-values at the `r fmt(1 / (B_test + 1))` simulation floor. These values are not exact zero probabilities, and smaller p-values from procedures that omit observed dependence do not override the primary calibration. Part III evaluates that issue under controlled data-generating processes.

## Calendar-time HAC standard errors for slope intervals

Confidence intervals generate data under the **fitted broken alternative**, rather than the null. Each draw repeats the date search and re-estimates both slopes. Percentile intervals use the bootstrap slope quantiles. Studentized percentile-$t$ intervals also recompute a standard error in every draw.

The local Jacobian contains the date derivative:

$$J_i=[1,x_i,(x_i-\tau)_+,-\widehat\delta\mathbf 1(x_i>\tau)],\qquad \tau=x_{\widehat k}.$$

For numerical stability, the fourth column is rescaled to the indicator $\mathbf 1(x_i>\tau)$. With a nonzero slope change, this does not change the covariance of the first three coefficients. The pre- and post-break contrasts are $(0,1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,1,0)$.

The calendar Bartlett kernel is $K_{ij}=\max\{1-|s_i-s_j|/7,0\}$. Only observed pairs exactly one to six calendar years apart enter the lag terms. The finite-sample multiplier is $n/(n-4)$, counting the local date parameter as well as the three regression coefficients. This is a local HAC approximation, and weak date identification can limit coverage.
```{r calendar-hac-standard-errors}
calendar_hac_se <- function(year, X, e, L=6) {
  n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X); A <- solve(crossprod(X))
  C <- cbind(c(0,1,0,0),c(0,1,1,0))
  influence <- (X %*% A %*% C)*as.numeric(e)
  v <- colSums(influence^2)
  for (lag in seq_len(L)) {
    j <- match(year+lag,year); i <- which(!is.na(j))
    if(length(i)) v <- v+2*(1-lag/(L+1))*colSums(influence[i,,drop=FALSE]*influence[j[i],,drop=FALSE])
  }
  sqrt(pmax(v*n/(n-p),.Machine$double.eps))
}
```

## Generate alternative samples and reselect the break

The alternative residual scaling uses three linear coefficients, while the local sandwich uses four parameters including the date; these corrections serve different roles. The bootstrap loop records reselected dates, slope estimates and their HAC standard errors, making the reported intervals independently reconstructible.

```{r confidence-interval-refits}
# Alternative bootstrap: both break location and slope estimates are refitted.
set.seed(seed+301L)
err<-bootstrap_errors(e1,year,B_ci,method="dwb",ell=6,df=3)
Ystar<-as.numeric(fitted(m1))+err
coefstar<-sestar<-matrix(NA_real_,B_ci,2); breakyears<-integer(B_ci)
seobs<-calendar_hac_se(year,cbind(X1,as.numeric(x>x[k])),e1)
for (b in seq_len(B_ci)) {
  ff<-fit_break(Ystar[,b],design); kk<-ff$index
  XX<-cbind(1,x,pmax(0,x-x[kk])); fit<-lm.fit(XX,Ystar[,b])
  coefstar[b,]<-c(fit$coefficients[2],sum(fit$coefficients[2:3]))
  sestar[b,]<-calendar_hac_se(year,cbind(XX,as.numeric(x>x[kk])),fit$residuals)
  breakyears[b]<-year[kk]
}
```

For either slope $\theta$, the percentile interval is
$[q_{.025}(\widehat\theta^*),q_{.975}(\widehat\theta^*)]$.
For the studentized interval, calculate

$$t^*=\frac{\widehat\theta^*-\widehat\theta}{s^*},\qquad
[\widehat\theta-q_{.975}(t^*)s,\ \widehat\theta-q_{.025}(t^*)s].$$

CI quantiles use R's interpolated type 7. Notice the reversed quantile order in the studentized endpoints. Holding the selected date fixed in bootstrap samples would omit part of slope uncertainty.

```{r construct-confidence-intervals}
tstar<-sweep(sweep(coefstar,2,theta,"-"),c(1,2),sestar,"/")
cis<-do.call(rbind,lapply(1:2,function(j){
  pc<-quantile(coefstar[,j],c(.025,.975),type=7,names=FALSE)
  qt<-quantile(tstar[,j],c(.975,.025),type=7,names=FALSE)
  pt<-theta[j]-seobs[j]*qt
  data.frame(parameter=c("pre","post")[j],estimate=unname(theta[j]),hac_se=unname(seobs[j]),
             type=c("percentile","percentile_t"),lower=c(pc[1],pt[1]),upper=c(pc[2],pt[2]),B=B_ci)
}))
write_csv(cis,"tables/confidence_intervals.csv")
knitr::kable(cis, digits = 4, caption = "Nominal 95% intervals in degrees C per decade")
```

Both pre-break intervals include zero, so the negative point estimate does not establish early cooling. Both post-break intervals exclude zero, supporting a positive later slope **conditional on the broken-trend framework**. These intervals are not a separate test establishing that a break exists, and the simulation below does not evaluate interval coverage.

```{r slope_intervals-plot, fig.cap="Percentile and percentile-t intervals; the vertical reference marks zero slope.", out.width="100%"}

```

## Model comparison and residual diagnostics

RSS, in-sample RMSE and $R^2$ describe fit. A searched model is more flexible, so improvement alone is not selection-adjusted evidence. The bootstrap addresses that distinction. The broken residuals should also be inspected rather than assuming that a new mean model removes dependence.

```{r model-comparison}
diagnostic<-function(m,label){
  e<-resid(m); bb<-n*summary(lm(e^2~x))$r.squared
  data.frame(model=label,RSS=sum(e^2),RMSE=sqrt(mean(e^2)),R2=summary(m)$r.squared,
    adjusted_R2=summary(m)$adj.r.squared,DW=sum(diff(e)^2)/sum(e^2),
    acf1=acf(e,plot=FALSE)$acf[2],BP=bb,BP_p=pchisq(bb,1,lower.tail=FALSE))
}
dg<-rbind(diagnostic(m0,"linear"),diagnostic(m1,"broken"))
write_csv(dg,"tables/model_diagnostics.csv")
knitr::kable(dg, digits = 4, caption = "Fit measures and remaining residual dependence")
```

The reduction in RSS is `r fmt(100 * Fobs / sum(e0^2), 2)`%. RMSE falls from `r fmt(dg$RMSE[1], 3)` to `r fmt(dg$RMSE[2], 3)` °C, and $R^2$ rises from `r fmt(dg$R2[1], 3)` to `r fmt(dg$R2[2], 3)`. Observation-lag ACF(1) falls to `r fmt(dg$acf1[2], 3)`, but dependence remains. Most annual variation is still unexplained.

```{r diagnostics_broken-plot, fig.cap="Residual diagnostics after selecting the broken trend; dependence remains visible.", out.width="100%"}

    par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.7), mgp = c(2.5, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.8)
    plot(year, e1, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = gray, xlab = "Calendar year", ylab = "Residual (degrees C)", 
        main = "Broken-trend residuals")

        col = navy)

    plot(year, e1^2, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = gray, xlab = "Calendar year", ylab = "Squared residual (degrees C squared)", 
        main = "Residual variance")
    lines(lowess(year, e1^2, f = 0.3), col = teal, lwd = 2)
    qqnorm(e1, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = gray, main = "Normal QQ plot", ylab = "Residual quantile (degrees C)")
    qqline(e1, col = teal, lwd = 2)
```

## Secondary sample sensitivity

Two descriptive checks omit the coldest observation in 1851 or end the sample in 1980, excluding the four observations after the long gap. Each check reselects the break using 15% trimming. These are point-estimate sensitivities, not new bootstrap significance tests. Every primary result above retains the complete supplied sample.

```{r sample-sensitivity}
# Secondary diagnostics only: retain the complete sample for every primary result.
sensitivities <- list(no_coldest = which(year != 1851), pre_gap = which(year <= 1980))

ss <- lapply(names(sensitivities), function(label) {
    ii <- sensitivities[[label]]
    fit <- fit_break(y[ii], prepare_design(year[ii]))
    xx <- (year[ii] - mean(year[ii]))/10
    mm <- lm(y[ii] ~ xx + I(pmax(0, xx - xx[fit$index])))
    data.frame(sample = label, n = length(ii), break_year = year[ii][fit$index], pre = coef(mm)[2], 
        post = sum(coef(mm)[2:3]), F = fit$F)
})

write_csv(do.call(rbind, ss), "tables/sample_sensitivity.csv")

sample_sensitivity <- read.csv("tables/sample_sensitivity.csv")

knitr::kable(sample_sensitivity, digits = 4)

```

Removing 1851 shifts the selected date slightly; ending in 1980 also preserves a positive later fitted slope. This suggests the fitted shape is not entirely attributable to the coldest year or the final four observations. It does not resolve unknown station history, model selection or missing decades.

# 9. Simulation Study of Bootstrap Procedures (Part III)

## Data-generating process and experimental factors

The simulation uses 226 equally spaced annual observations and a central true break at index 113:

$$y_t=9.5-0.05x_t+\delta(x_t-x_{113})_++\varepsilon_t,\quad
x_t=(t-\bar t)/10,$$

$$\varepsilon_t=\rho\varepsilon_{t-1}+\sigma_tu_t,\qquad u_t\sim N(0,1).$$

Eight scenarios cross $\delta\in\{0,0.14\}$, $\rho\in\{0,0.4\}$ and constant or increasing innovation scale. When $\delta=0$, rejection frequency estimates **size** under the no-break null; when $\delta=0.14$, it estimates **power**. The slope change approximates the empirical estimate.

The common innovation scale is calibrated from the empirical broken-model residual standard deviation, $\widehat\sigma=\sqrt{RSS_1/(n-3)}$. For the increasing profile, scales ranging from 0.5 to 1.5 are normalized to have mean square one. This matches average innovation variance across scale conditions; it does not fix marginal error variance across values of $\rho$.

Initialization is stationary for constant scale and a local initialization for changing scale. Unlike the empirical design, the simulated calendar has no missing years; it isolates the selected dependence and variance factors.

```{r simulation-data-generator}
simulate_broken_trend <- function(design, delta, rho, heteroskedastic,
                                  sigma, alpha = 9.5, beta = -0.05,
                                  break_index = floor(design$n / 2)) {
  n <- design$n
  scale_profile <- if (heteroskedastic) seq(0.5, 1.5, length.out = n) else rep(1, n)
  # Match average innovation variance across variance-profile conditions.
  scale_profile <- scale_profile / sqrt(mean(scale_profile^2))
  sigma_t <- sigma * scale_profile
  u <- rnorm(n)
  error <- numeric(n)
  # Stationary initialization under the initial innovation scale. For changing
  # sigma_t this is a local initialization, not global stationarity.
  error[1L] <- sigma_t[1L] * u[1L] / sqrt(1 - rho^2)
  for (i in 2L:n) error[i] <- rho * error[i - 1L] + sigma_t[i] * u[i]
  alpha + beta * design$x +
    delta * pmax(0, design$x - design$x[break_index]) + error
}
```

## Monte Carlo uncertainty

If $r$ of $M$ datasets reject, the rejection frequency is $\widehat p=r/M$ and its Monte Carlo standard error is $\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/M}$. We also report Wilson intervals. Unlike a plug-in standard error, these remain informative at a rejection rate of 100%. They measure uncertainty in simulation frequencies, not empirical slope uncertainty.

```{r wilson-interval}
wilson_interval <- function(successes, trials, level = 0.95) {
  z <- qnorm((1 + level) / 2)
  p <- successes / trials
  den <- 1 + z^2 / trials
  ctr <- (p + z^2 / (2 * trials)) / den
  half <- z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / trials + z^2 / (4 * trials^2)) / den
  c(lower = max(0, ctr - half), upper = min(1, ctr + half))
}
```

## Run and checkpoint all scenarios

Every scenario uses $M=1,000$ datasets, and each dataset receives all three bootstrap tests with $B=499$. This totals 8,000 datasets, 24,000 tests and 11,976,000 bootstrap draws. DWB uses bandwidth six.

Dataset $m$ in scenario $c$ receives seed $20260926+100000c+m$. Consequently, changing worker scheduling does not change its random stream. Methods use the same simulated datasets. Each complete scenario is checkpointed together with every setting affecting its statistical computation. Checkpoints with changed settings are recomputed, and an incomplete scenario is not accepted.

```{r simulation-engine}
run_simulation <- function(M = 1000L, B = 499L, n = 226L,
                           sigma = NULL, seed = 20260926L,
                           workers = min(4L, parallel::detectCores()),
                           checkpoint_dir = "work/simulation",
                           summary_file = "tables/simulation_summary.csv",
                           raw_file = "work/simulation/simulation_results.rds",
                           resume = TRUE) {
  if (is.null(sigma)) {
    station <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "Station08.csv"))
    station <- station[order(station$Year), ]
    empirical <- fit_break(station$Temperature, prepare_design(station$Year))
    sigma <- sqrt(empirical$RSS1 / (nrow(station) - 3L))
  }
  stopifnot(M >= 1000L, B >= 499L, n >= 10L, sigma > 0, workers >= 1L)
  design <- prepare_design(seq_len(n), trim = 0.15)
  settings <- list(M = as.integer(M), B = as.integer(B), n = as.integer(n),
                   sigma = sigma, seed = as.integer(seed), alpha = 9.5,
                   beta = -0.05, break_index = floor(n / 2),
                   trim = 0.15, level = 0.05, ell = round(n^(1/3)),
                   statistic = "raw RSS reduction", engine_version = 1L)
  scenarios <- expand.grid(delta = c(0, 0.14), rho = c(0, 0.4),
                           heteroskedastic = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                           KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
  scenarios$config <- seq_len(nrow(scenarios))
  dir.create(checkpoint_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  dir.create(dirname(summary_file), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  dir.create(dirname(raw_file), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  all_raw <- vector("list", nrow(scenarios))
  start <- Sys.time()
  for (s in seq_len(nrow(scenarios))) {
    scenario <- scenarios[s, ]
    signature <- list(settings = settings, scenario = scenario)
    checkpoint <- file.path(checkpoint_dir, sprintf("config_%02d.rds", s))
    cached <- if (resume && file.exists(checkpoint)) readRDS(checkpoint) else NULL
    if (!is.null(cached) && identical(cached$signature, signature) &&
        nrow(cached$raw) == M) {
      all_raw[[s]] <- cached$raw
      message(sprintf("Scenario %d/8: reused verified complete checkpoint.", s))
      next
    }
    one_replication <- function(replication) {
      # Seeds do not depend on worker scheduling or the number of workers.
      replicate_seed <- as.integer(seed + s * 100000L + replication)
      set.seed(replicate_seed)
      y <- simulate_broken_trend(design, delta = scenario$delta,
                                 rho = scenario$rho,
                                 heteroskedastic = scenario$heteroskedastic,
                                 sigma = sigma)
      fit <- bootstrap_break(y, design, B = B, ell = settings$ell,
                             level = settings$level)
      out <- c(replication = replication, replicate_seed = replicate_seed,
               F = fit$observed$F, estimated_break_index = fit$observed$index)
      for (method in c("iid", "wild", "dwb")) {
        out[paste0(method, "_p")] <- fit$results[[method]]$p_value
        out[paste0(method, "_critical")] <- fit$results[[method]]$critical
        out[paste0(method, "_reject")] <- as.integer(fit$results[[method]]$reject)
      }
      out
    }
    replications <- if (.Platform$OS.type != "windows" && workers > 1L) {
      parallel::mclapply(seq_len(M), one_replication, mc.cores = workers,
                        mc.preschedule = TRUE, mc.set.seed = FALSE)
    } else lapply(seq_len(M), one_replication)
    if (any(vapply(replications, inherits, logical(1), "try-error")))
      stop("A simulation worker failed; no incomplete scenario was saved.")
    raw <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, replications))
    raw$config <- s
    raw$delta <- scenario$delta
    raw$rho <- scenario$rho
    raw$heteroskedastic <- scenario$heteroskedastic
    all_raw[[s]] <- raw
    saveRDS(list(signature = signature, raw = raw), checkpoint, version = 3)
    message(sprintf("Scenario %d/8 complete: delta=%.2f, rho=%.1f, heteroskedastic=%s; elapsed %.1f s.",
                    s, scenario$delta, scenario$rho, scenario$heteroskedastic,
                    as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), start, units = "secs"))))
  }
  raw <- do.call(rbind, all_raw)
  rownames(raw) <- NULL
  summaries <- list()
  i <- 0L
  for (s in seq_len(nrow(scenarios))) for (method in c("iid", "wild", "dwb")) {
    i <- i + 1L
    subsample <- raw[raw$config == s, ]
    rejections <- sum(subsample[[paste0(method, "_reject")]])
    rate <- rejections / M
    interval <- wilson_interval(rejections, M)
    summaries[[i]] <- data.frame(config = s, delta = scenarios$delta[s],
      rho = scenarios$rho[s], heteroskedastic = scenarios$heteroskedastic[s],
      estimand = if (scenarios$delta[s] == 0) "size" else "power", method = method,
      M = M, B = B, n = n, sigma = sigma, seed = seed, ell = settings$ell,
      rejections = rejections, rejection_rate = rate,
      mc_se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / M),
      lower_95 = unname(interval[1L]), upper_95 = unname(interval[2L]))
  }
  summary <- do.call(rbind, summaries)
  result <- list(settings = settings, scenarios = scenarios, raw = raw,
                 summary = summary, elapsed_seconds =
                   as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), start, units = "secs")),
                 session_info = sessionInfo())
  write.csv(summary, summary_file, row.names = FALSE)
  saveRDS(result, raw_file, version = 3)
  message(sprintf("Saved %d replications, %d bootstrap tests, and %d summary rows.",
                  nrow(raw), nrow(raw) * 3L, nrow(summary)))
  invisible(result)
}
```

The next chunk can copy the existing project checkpoints into the separate Rmd working area. It never writes to the original checkpoint files. The simulation engine verifies their settings before reuse. If fresh computation is requested, copied or previously generated checkpoints are ignored.

```{r run-simulation, message=TRUE}
checkpoint_dir <- file.path("work", "simulation")
if (!params$recompute_simulation) {
  original_checkpoints <- list.files(
    file.path(project_root, "work", "simulation"),
    pattern = "^config_[0-9]{2}\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE
  )
  for (original in original_checkpoints) {
    target <- file.path(checkpoint_dir, basename(original))
    if (!file.exists(target)) {
      copied <- file.copy(original, target, overwrite = FALSE)
      if (!copied) stop("Could not copy a simulation checkpoint: ", original)
    }
  }
}
sigma <- sqrt(fast$RSS1 / (n - 3L))
simulation <- run_simulation(
  M = simulation_M, B = simulation_B, n = n,
  sigma = sigma, seed = master_seed, workers = workers,
  checkpoint_dir = checkpoint_dir,
  summary_file = "tables/simulation_summary.csv",
  raw_file = "work/simulation/simulation_results.rds",
  resume = !params$recompute_simulation
)
sim <- simulation$summary
knitr::kable(simulation$scenarios, caption = "Eight Monte Carlo configurations")
cat("Calibrated innovation scale:", sigma, "degrees C\n")
cat("Datasets:", nrow(simulation$raw),
    "; bootstrap tests:", 3L * nrow(simulation$raw),
    "; bootstrap samples:", 3L * nrow(simulation$raw) * simulation_B, "\n")
```

## Rejection frequencies and their interpretation

A well-calibrated nominal 5% test should reject approximately 5% of no-break datasets. Power must be interpreted alongside size: a method that rejects too often under the null can have misleadingly high apparent power.

```{r simulation-results-table}
method_names <- c(iid = "IID residual", wild = "Independent wild", dwb = "Dependent wild")
simulation_comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(sim$config), function(config) {
  z <- sim[sim$config == config, ]
  rates <- vapply(c("iid", "wild", "dwb"), function(method) {
    100 * z$rejection_rate[z$method == method]
  }, numeric(1L))
  data.frame(
    Configuration = config, Quantity = ifelse(z$delta[1] == 0, "Size", "Power"),
    Change = z$delta[1], Rho = z$rho[1],
    Innovation_scale = ifelse(z$heteroskedastic[1], "Increasing", "Constant"),
    IID_residual_percent = rates[1], Independent_wild_percent = rates[2],
    Dependent_wild_percent = rates[3], row.names = NULL
  )
}))
knitr::kable(simulation_comparison, digits = 1, caption = "Rejection frequencies (%)")
```

With independent, constant-variance errors, IID residual and independent wild tests have sizes 4.1% and 4.3%. Under independence and increasing variance, IID residual size rises to 8.8%, while independent wild remains near nominal at 5.4%.

Serial correlation has a larger effect. At $\rho=0.4$, the independent procedures reject 26.5–32.2% of no-break datasets across the scale designs. Their resampling schemes remove the serial dependence affecting the observed search statistic, making the simulated critical values too small in these settings.

DWB null rejection rates are 2.1–3.5%. It avoids over-rejection here but is conservative relative to 5%, rather than exactly calibrated. Its power is 98.5–99.0% under independence and 74.6–78.5% with autocorrelation. Higher apparent power from the independent methods under serial correlation should not be read as superior performance because their null sizes are distorted. Size-adjusted power is not calculated.

```{r simulation-results-plot, fig.cap="Size and power; vertical lines are Wilson intervals for simulation frequencies."}
plot_pair("simulation_results", function() {
    par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5.2, 4.4, 2.4, 0.8), mgp = c(2.7, 0.7, 0), las = 1, cex = 0.8)
    cols <- c("#667781", "#174A6E", "#00857D")
    for (estimand in c("size", "power")) {
        z <- sim[sim$estimand == estimand, ]
        ks <- unique(z$config)
        ylim <- if (estimand == "size") 
            c(0, 40)
        else c(60, 103)
        plot(1, 1, type = "n", xlim = c(0.6, 4.4), ylim = ylim, xaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "Rejection frequency (%)", 
            main = ifelse(estimand == "size", "Null rejection (nominal 5%)", "Power (change 0.14 degrees C/decade)"))
        axis(1, at = 1:4, labels = c("Independent\nconstant", "AR(0.4)\nconstant", "Independent\nincreasing", 
            "AR(0.4)\nincreasing"), tick = FALSE, cex.axis = 0.8)
        if (estimand == "size") 
            abline(h = 5, lty = 3, col = "#8F999E")
        for (j in 1:3) {
            zz <- z[z$method == c("iid", "wild", "dwb")[j], ]
            xx <- (1:4) + (j - 2) * 0.1
            lines(xx, 100 * zz$rejection_rate, type = "b", pch = 15 + j, col = cols[j], lwd = 1.4)
            segments(xx, 100 * zz$lower_95, xx, 100 * zz$upper_95, col = cols[j])
        }
        if (estimand == "size") 
            legend("topleft", c("IID residual", "Independent wild", "Dependent wild"), col = cols, 
                pch = 16:18, lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
    }
}, 10, 4.6)

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(artifact_root, "figures/simulation_results.png"))

```

The simulation supports retaining dependence in station inference, but it does not prove that the empirical DWB p-value is conservative. It covers Gaussian innovations, one sample size, one reasonably strong central kink and one DWB bandwidth. It does not evaluate missingness, weak or multiple breaks, alternative dependence models or confidence-interval coverage. Those limits temper direct transfer to the irregular empirical record.


# 10. Independent Validation and Project Conclusion

The checks below are executable, not a list of asserted results. They compare optimized search statistics with brute-force regressions, reconstruct both interval types from all stored refits, verify empirical p-value corrections, reconstruct every simulation rejection frequency and Wilson interval, and independently replay one complete dataset from each of the eight scenarios.

All functions used by the checks are defined in this Rmd. Validation writes only inside its own working area.


## Check the retained Part I computations

These checks verify that the year-1900 centering preserves the fitted line, that the complete supplied sample is retained, that an independent QR projection reproduces all 9,999 draws for both DW definitions, and that the one-regressor BP statistic agrees with its squared-correlation identity.

```{r part1-independent-checks}
original_data <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "Station08.csv"))
stopifnot(identical(dat$Year, original_data$Year),
          identical(dat$Temperature, original_data$Temperature),
          n == 226L, length(missing_years) == 35L, nrow(gap_table) == 5L)
centered_model <- lm(Temperature ~ I((Year - mean(Year)) / 10), data = dat)
stopifnot(max(abs(fitted(centered_model) - fitted(trend_model))) < 1e-10,
          abs(coef(centered_model)[2] - beta1_hat) < 1e-12,
          abs(coef(centered_model)[1] + beta1_hat * (1900 - mean(dat$Year)) / 10 - beta0_hat) < 1e-12)

set.seed(master_seed)
Z_check <- matrix(rnorm(n * B), nrow = n)
Q_check <- qr.Q(qr(model.matrix(trend_model)))
E_check <- Z_check - Q_check %*% crossprod(Q_check, Z_check)
dw_replayed <- colSums((E_check[-1, , drop = FALSE] -
                        E_check[-n, , drop = FALSE])^2) / colSums(E_check^2)
dw_gap_replayed <- colSums((E_check[valid_pairs + 1L, , drop = FALSE] -
                            E_check[valid_pairs, , drop = FALSE])^2) / colSums(E_check^2)
stopifnot(max(abs(dw_replayed - d_sim)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(dw_gap_replayed - d_sim_gap)) < 1e-10,
          abs(n * cor(dat$residual_sq, dat$t)^2 - BP_stat) < 1e-12)
part1_checks <- c(
  "PASS: all supplied rows, five gaps and 35 missing years are retained",
  "PASS: year-1900 and mean-year parameterizations have identical fitted lines and slopes",
  "PASS: independent QR projection reproduces both 9,999-draw DW reference distributions",
  "PASS: BP agrees with the one-regressor squared-correlation identity"
)
write_csv(dw_results, "tables/dw_comparison.csv")
writeLines(part1_checks, "outputs/part1_validation.txt")
cat(paste(part1_checks, collapse = "\n"), "\n")
```

```{r independent-validation}
    stopifnot(all(values >= 1 / 500 & values <= 1),
              all(abs(500 * values - round(500 * values)) < 1e-8))
    row <- summary[summary$config == s & summary$method == method, ]
    count <- sum(values <= .05)
    rate <- count / 1000
    interval <- wilson_interval(count, 1000)
    stopifnot(row$rejections == count, abs(row$rejection_rate - rate) < 1e-12,
      abs(row$mc_se - sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / 1000)) < 1e-12,
      max(abs(c(row$lower_95, row$upper_95) - interval)) < 1e-12)
  }
}
pass("all 8,000 replications, 24 rejection rates, MC standard errors and Wilson intervals are consistent")

# Replay one observation from every scenario, independently of worker scheduling.
Ds <- prepare_design(seq_len(226L))
for (s in seq_len(8L)) {
  row <- raw[raw$config == s & raw$replication == 1000L, ]
  set.seed(row$replicate_seed)
  ys <- simulate_broken_trend(Ds, row$delta, row$rho, row$heteroskedastic,
                              simulation$settings$sigma)
  result <- bootstrap_break(ys, Ds, B = 499L)
  stopifnot(abs(result$observed$F - row$F) < 1e-10)
  for (method in c("iid", "wild", "dwb"))
    stopifnot(abs(result$results[[method]]$p_value - row[[paste0(method, "_p")]]) < 1e-12)
}
pass("recorded seeds reproduce one complete replication from every simulation scenario")
writeLines(checks, "outputs/validation.txt")
cat("All checks passed. Saved outputs/validation.txt.\n")
```



## Conclusion of the completed project

The complete Station08 record has a positive descriptive linear slope, but the initial model leaves residual dependence and low-frequency mean departures. A continuous broken trend fits best at `r year[k]` and reduces RSS by `r fmt(100 * Fobs / sum(e0^2), 2)`%. Its estimated pre- and post-break slopes are `r fmt(coef(m1)[2])` and `r fmt(sum(coef(m1)[2:3]))`°C per decade.

Both early-slope interval constructions include zero. Both later-slope intervals exclude zero, conditional on the broken-trend framework. Evidence about the existence of a break is more qualified: the primary six-year DWB bandwidth rejects at 5%, while the twelve-year bandwidth does not. A best-fitting date should therefore not be interpreted as an established historical or physical event.

The Monte Carlo experiment shows why independent-error bootstrap procedures can over-reject when errors are persistent. DWB avoids that distortion in the studied scenarios but is conservative and has lower power under dependence. This does not prove that its empirical p-value is conservative. Missing years, unknown station history, other possible mean and dependence structures, and the absence of a CI coverage study remain limitations.

## Seeds and session information

Part I and its independent replay use seed `r master_seed`. Empirical IID, independent wild and primary DWB tests use master seed `20260926` plus 101, 102 and 103. The bandwidth checks use master plus 203 and 212, and slope intervals use master plus 301. Simulation dataset $m$ in scenario $c$ uses `20260926 + 100000*c + m`, independently of worker scheduling.

# Appendix 1: Choosing the Centric Year


The year 1900 is retained as a familiar reference inside the observed period. It makes the intercept easy to describe and the decade scaling makes the slope easy to read. Moving the center to the sample mean would change the intercept but leave the fitted curve, slope, RSS and break search unchanged. Under independent homoskedastic OLS, centering at the sample mean minimizes the intercept's classical variance; that observation does not validate independent-error standard errors for this series. The choice of 1900 is a communication convention, not evidence of a pre-industrial baseline.

# Appendix 2: Impact of Data Gaps on This Analysis — Summary


| Component | Effect of gaps | Approach retained or refined |
|---|---|---|
| Exploratory and residual time plots | Observed lines must not imply data inside gaps | Lines are grouped by contiguous years; the largest gap is shaded |
| OLS estimates | Calendar spacing is represented, but coverage and missingness can matter | Retain $(\mathrm{Year}-1900)/10$ and the complete supplied sample |
| Residual ACF | Observation lags and calendar lags differ | Display both; calendar grid contains `NA` for absent years |
| Variance smooth | Its curve inside a gap is unsupported by observations there | Retain the descriptive smooth with an explicit limitation |
| QQ plot | Time order is absent from its construction | Treat it as a marginal descriptive comparison, not proof of Gaussianity |
| DW statistic and Monte Carlo | Assignment formula uses observation adjacency | Primary assigned statistic plus separately calibrated calendar-adjacent sensitivity |
| BP test | Algebra uses actual time; dependence qualifies its reference | Retain $nR^2$ and nominal $\chi^2_1$, with cautious non-rejection language |
| Part II bootstrap | Dependence should use actual calendar gaps | DWB multipliers depend on elapsed years; every sample repeats the date search |
| Overall interpretation | Missing decades and metadata limit conclusions | No inference about an unobserved trajectory, global change or physical cause |
